title: Endocrine: Low Sugar, High-Sugar Crises, Thyroid

questions.stem: An awake client has a blood sugar of 58 mg/dL and is shaky. What is the first action?

options.text: Give 15 g of fast sugar, like half a cup of juice

questions.explanation: A is correct: 58 is below 70, the client is awake and can swallow, so give 15 g of fast sugar, then recheck in 15 minutes. B would drop the sugar further. C delays treatment. D, a full meal, is too slow to start with.

questions.stem: After giving 15 g of fast sugar for low blood sugar, when should the nurse recheck?
questions.explanation: B is correct: the 15-15 rule is 15 g of fast sugar, wait 15 minutes, then recheck. A is too soon. C and D are too late.

questions.stem: A client with low blood sugar cannot swallow safely. What does the nurse expect to give?

options.text: Glucagon or intravenous dextrose, as ordered

questions.explanation: C is correct: if the client can't swallow safely, give glucagon or intravenous dextrose, as ordered. A and B need safe swallowing. D would lower blood sugar further.

questions.stem: Which findings suggest low blood sugar? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: A, B, C, and D are correct: these are the taught signs of low blood sugar. E, fruity breath, is a sign of diabetic ketoacidosis.

questions.stem: A client with type 1 diabetes has fruity breath, deep fast breathing, a blood sugar of 450, and ketones. What is most likely?
questions.explanation: B is correct: type 1, fruity breath, deep fast breathing, high sugar, and ketones point to diabetic ketoacidosis. A is usually type 2 with few ketones. C and D don't fit high sugar and ketones.

questions.stem: Per the 2024 consensus criteria shown in the video, which findings support diabetic ketoacidosis? Select all that apply.

options.text: Blood sugar 200 mg/dL or higher, or known diabetes

questions.explanation: A, B, and C are correct: the board shows glucose 200 or higher or known diabetes, a ketone level of 3.0 or higher, and pH under 7.3 or bicarb under 18. D describes the very high sugar common in hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state. E is wrong because ketones are part of diabetic ketoacidosis.

questions.stem: Which finding best distinguishes hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state from diabetic ketoacidosis?

options.text: Severe dehydration with blood sugar often over 600 and few ketones
Deep, fast breathing to blow off acid

questions.explanation: B is correct: hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state is usually type 2, with sugar often over 600, severe dehydration, and not much ketones. A, C, and D describe diabetic ketoacidosis.

questions.stem: A client in diabetic ketoacidosis has a potassium of 3.2 mEq/L after intravenous fluids were started. An insulin infusion is ordered. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Replace potassium first and hold insulin until potassium is above 3.5
Give the insulin as a push

questions.explanation: B is correct: a potassium of 3.2 is below 3.5, so replace it first and hold insulin until it's above 3.5, because insulin pushes potassium into the cells. A and C give insulin with low potassium. D stops the first-line treatment.

questions.stem: What is the first treatment for both diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state?
questions.explanation: B is correct: for both, intravenous fluids come first. A comes after fluids and a potassium check. C is wrong because drinking can't replace a large fluid loss quickly enough. D is wrong because potassium is never pushed.

questions.stem: Which set of findings fits low thyroid?

options.text: Anxious, hot, weight loss, fast pulse
Tired, cold, weight gain, slow pulse
Shaky and sweaty with low sugar

questions.explanation: B is correct: low thyroid slows everything down: tired, cold, weight gain, and a slow pulse. A is high thyroid. C is diabetic ketoacidosis. D is low blood sugar.
